extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, law, and theology; scholars and statesmen interested in civil sovereignty and legal-political doctrine
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and procedural standards about when and how individuals become subjects of a conqueror, limits on private violence, the duties of subjects in war, and related grounding of sovereign and ecclesiastical authority (as argued in Hobbes' Leviathan).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coexistence of judgment and fancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgment and Fancy may have place in the same man, but by turns; education and discipline can reconcile them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author gives analogies (Israelites sometimes fixed to brick-making, sometimes ranging to gather straw) to show faculties operate at different times; implication: cultivate education/discipline to allow reason and imagination to function as required by ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of both Reason and Eloquence in deliberations
rubrics_metrics.description: In all deliberations and pleadings, solid Reasoning is necessary for just resolutions, and powerful Eloquence is necessary to procure attention and consent; they are contrary faculties—Reason grounded on principles of Truth, Eloquence on received Opinions, Passions and Interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without Reason, resolutions are rash and unjust; without Eloquence, the effect of Reason will be little. Recognize the tension and manage both faculties according to the end sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions alter public duty (courage and timorousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courage (contempt of wounds and violent death) inclines men to private revenges and may unsettle public peace; Timorousness often disposes men to desert the public defence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These passions have opposite civic effects and generally do not co-exist strongly in one person; consider passion dispositions when evaluating conduct, leadership, or laws addressing revenge and duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to protect the authority that protects you
rubrics_metrics.description: Every man is bound by nature, as much as in him lieth, to protect in war the Authority by which he is himself protected in time of peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One who claims a right of self-preservation cannot claim a right to destroy the power that preserves him; this is a manifest contradiction and grounds a duty of defence of sovereign authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a person becomes subject to a conqueror: consent requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A man becomes subject to a conqueror at the point when, having the liberty to submit, he consents—either by express words or by other sufficient sign—to be his subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consent may be express or tacit; the timing depends on having liberty to submit (see next metric). This establishes voluntary submission (actual or tacit) as the constitutive act creating subjection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty to submit defined (means of life within enemy protection)
rubrics_metrics.description: For one who has no obligation to his former sovereign beyond that of an ordinary subject, liberty to submit exists when his means of life are within the guards and garrisons of the enemy; he then no longer receives protection from his former sovereign but from the adverse party for his contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because contribution to the enemy is inevitable under such circumstances (and is treated as lawful), total submission (composition) cannot be deemed unlawful; this explains a factual condition creating liberty to submit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soldier exception to liberty to submit
rubrics_metrics.description: If, besides ordinary subject obligations, a man has taken upon him the new obligation of a soldier, he may not lawfully submit to a new power while the old one keeps the field and provides subsistence; when that also fails, a soldier may seek protection elsewhere and lawfully submit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A contract lawfully made (soldier's duty) cannot be broken while the old sovereign provides the means of subsistence; once those means fail, the soldier may change allegiance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Conquest and acquisition of sovereign right
rubrics_metrics.description: Conquest is not mere victory but the acquisition by victory of a Right over the persons of men; one is conquered when, upon promise of obedience, life and liberty are allowed—i.e., when the people contract with the victor promising obedience for life and liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Victory (overcoming) is distinct from conquest (acquiring sovereignty). The Roman example (pacifying a province via promises to 'do what the Roman people command') illustrates how express and tacit promises create sovereign rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tacit vs express submission; living under protection as tacit submission
rubrics_metrics.description: The promise binding subjects may be express or tacit: living openly under the protection of the victor is understood as tacit submission; living secretly under such protection renders one liable to punishment as a spy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tacit submission arises from public, open conduct under the victor's protection; secret dependence does not confer the protections of submission and may expose one to penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence during conquest does not create subjection
rubrics_metrics.description: If a man is out of the country when it is conquered, he is not conquered nor subject; if upon his return he submits to the government, he then becomes bound to obey it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes being overcome (defeated) from being conquered (made subject by promise/consent). Presence and subsequent conduct determine legal status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of requiring approbation of past actions by conquerors
rubrics_metrics.description: A seed of dissolution is when conquerors require not only future submission but also approbation of their past actions; since few beginnings of commonwealths can be justified in conscience, demanding this breeds instability and justifies rebellion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political prudence: founders should not insist on retroactive justification of their acts as a condition of submission; doing so undermines long-term legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private zeal does not justify killing; executions require public judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripture and law do not countenance executions by private zeal; executions in the commonwealth must proceed by public sentence and due process—private killings are often products of ignorance and passion and contravene justice and peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Levites killing at Golden Calf acted by Moses' command; Phinehas’s killing was ratified by Moses; otherwise private zeal lacks lawful authority. Extrajudicial violence is not acceptable unless ratified by public authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mosaic procedural requirements for capital punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Mosaic law, the convicted of a capital crime should be stoned by the people, with the witnesses casting the first stone; witnesses must be heard before execution unless the fact was committed in presence of the congregation or judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process against idolatry (Deut. 13) requires diligent inquiry and conviction before execution; witness-first-stone rule separates public condemnation from private zeal and provides procedural safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawful suppression of rebellion and later ratification
rubrics_metrics.description: In sudden rebellions, a person who suppresses the rebellion by his power may lawfully act in the moment and subsequently seek ratification or pardon; presumption of future ratification can be necessary for the safety of the commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an exception permitting extraordinary acts in emergency when delay would preclude effective suppression, provided subsequent public ratification or pardon is sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounding of civil and ecclesiastical authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The civil right of sovereigns is grounded on the known natural inclinations of mankind and the articles of the law of nature; the ecclesiastical power of sovereigns is grounded on scripture texts that are evident and consonant with the scope of scripture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author claims these grounds justify sovereign authority; acknowledges those already committed to contrary opinions will not be easily persuaded by this grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles for use of ancient authorities in argumentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth of doctrine depends on Reason or Scripture, not on quoting ancient poets, orators, and philosophers; matters of Right admit no place for witnesses—antiquity often contradicts, may be used fraudulently, and quoting unchewed Greek/Latin is an ornament of indigestion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author lists reasons to avoid reliance on antiquity: ancient writers contradict themselves and others; opinions taken on credit are not the citer's own; ancients did not consistently imitate predecessors; quoting may mask weak argument. Anti-pattern: preferring ancient authority over present reasoned truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation for teaching to secure public doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: The discourse may be profitably printed and taught in universities to purify civil and moral doctrine from 'venime of heathen politicians' and deceiving spirits, thereby reducing subjects' susceptibility to ambitious agitators and lowering burdens to maintain public liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universities as fountains of civil and moral doctrine should ensure purity of instruction so preachers and gentry convey sound doctrine to the people; pedagogical recommendation for institutional adoption.
